Usage

Quick start

git clone https://github.com/{{REPO_ORG}}/{{REPO_NAME}}.git
cd {{REPO_NAME}}
pixi install
pixi run snakemake --cores 1

(Pixi resolves pixi.toml against the per-platform pixi.lock, installs the env under .pixi/, and provides pixi run for any task without needing an activate step.)

Or with Docker:

docker run --rm ghcr.io/{{REPO_ORG}}/{{REPO_NAME}}:latest

The Jupyter Book version is at https://{{REPO_ORG}}.github.io/{{REPO_NAME}}/.

What you get

This template bakes in conventions that took multiple replications to discover. By using it, you inherit:

  • FAIR4RS conformance — see docs/fair4rs-checklist.md for the principle-by-principle mapping.
  • Self-contained data downloads — the first notebook fetches everything; no manual data prep.
  • pixi.toml + pixi.lock as single source of truth — local dev, Docker, and CI all install the same per-platform-pinned env.
  • prefix-dev/setup-pixi-based CI — caches the env, runs the pipeline with pixi run, executes notebooks via a glob, fails fast on a stale lockfile.
  • Jupyter Book deployment — auto-deploys to GitHub Pages with BASE_URL set correctly. (Don't put base_url in myst.yml — MyST silently ignores it.)
  • Docker + GHCR + Zenodo image archival — release trigger pushes to GHCR and (optionally) archives to Zenodo for long-term preservation.
  • RO-Crate packaging — the entire repo is a navigable Research Object via ro-crate-metadata.json (Process Run Crate + Workflow RO-Crate profiles).
  • Six-step FORRT chain workspace — nanopubs/drafts/ has a field-by-field skeleton for each step. nanopubs/PUBLISHED.md is the URI registry.
  • Layered AI guidance — CLAUDE.md (universal) + DOMAIN.md (swappable per field) + USER_PREFERENCES.md (per-user). See docs/ai-portability.md for non-Claude AI tools.
  • Sandbox by default — .claude/settings.json denies file ops outside the repo, so a fresh AI session can't accidentally read ~/.ssh/ or write to /etc/.

Usage

Quick start

git clone https://github.com/{{REPO_ORG}}/{{REPO_NAME}}.git
cd {{REPO_NAME}}
pixi install
pixi run snakemake --cores 1

(Pixi resolves pixi.toml against the per-platform pixi.lock, installs the env under .pixi/, and provides pixi run for any task without needing an activate step.)

Or with Docker:

docker run --rm ghcr.io/{{REPO_ORG}}/{{REPO_NAME}}:latest

The Jupyter Book version is at https://{{REPO_ORG}}.github.io/{{REPO_NAME}}/.

What you get

This template bakes in conventions that took multiple replications to discover. By using it, you inherit:

  • FAIR4RS conformance — see docs/fair4rs-checklist.md for the principle-by-principle mapping.
  • Self-contained data downloads — the first notebook fetches everything; no manual data prep.
  • pixi.toml + pixi.lock as single source of truth — local dev, Docker, and CI all install the same per-platform-pinned env.
  • prefix-dev/setup-pixi-based CI — caches the env, runs the pipeline with pixi run, executes notebooks via a glob, fails fast on a stale lockfile.
  • Jupyter Book deployment — auto-deploys to GitHub Pages with BASE_URL set correctly. (Don't put base_url in myst.yml — MyST silently ignores it.)
  • Docker + GHCR + Zenodo image archival — release trigger pushes to GHCR and (optionally) archives to Zenodo for long-term preservation.
  • RO-Crate packaging — the entire repo is a navigable Research Object via ro-crate-metadata.json (Process Run Crate + Workflow RO-Crate profiles).
  • Six-step FORRT chain workspace — nanopubs/drafts/ has a field-by-field skeleton for each step. nanopubs/PUBLISHED.md is the URI registry.
  • Layered AI guidance — CLAUDE.md (universal) + DOMAIN.md (swappable per field) + USER_PREFERENCES.md (per-user). See docs/ai-portability.md for non-Claude AI tools.
  • Sandbox by default — .claude/settings.json denies file ops outside the repo, so a fresh AI session can't accidentally read ~/.ssh/ or write to /etc/.

Usage

What the dashboard shows

  • Risk map (PFR) — aggregated HEALPix cells (public tier), rendered with MapLibre GL.
  • Context backgrounds — social vulnerability and vulnerability drivers.
  • Public / internal views — the server decides which tiers a deployment may see.
  • Evidence / metadata — provenance, data-access conditions and scholarly annotations read from the source RO-Crates.

Quick start

local:

git clone https://github.com/FAIR2Adapt/urban-pfr-dashboard.git
git clone https://github.com/FAIR2Adapt/fdo-consume.git
cd urban-pfr-dashboard
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate        # Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
pip install ../fdo-consume
python server.py

Docker:

docker compose up --build

open http://localhost:8000.

  • ?source=<id> opens one source, e.g. ?source=fdo-loom-record (Hamburg) or ?source=bremen-loom-record (Bremen).
  • MapLibre GL is the default renderer; without WebGL the map is drawn with Leaflet.
  • The synthetic test data for Hamburg and Bremen is in test-data/fdo-cca-demo; no data generation is needed.

Usage

What the dashboard shows

  • Risk map (PFR) — aggregated HEALPix cells (public tier), rendered with MapLibre GL.
  • Context backgrounds — social vulnerability and vulnerability drivers.
  • Public / internal views — the server decides which tiers a deployment may see.
  • Evidence / metadata — provenance, data-access conditions and scholarly annotations read from the source RO-Crates.

Quick start

local:

git clone https://github.com/FAIR2Adapt/urban-pfr-dashboard.git
git clone https://github.com/FAIR2Adapt/fdo-consume.git
cd urban-pfr-dashboard
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate        # Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
pip install ../fdo-consume
python server.py

Docker:

docker compose up --build

open http://localhost:8000.

  • ?source=<id> opens one source, e.g. ?source=fdo-loom-record (Hamburg) or ?source=bremen-loom-record (Bremen).
  • MapLibre GL is the default renderer; without WebGL the map is drawn with Leaflet.
  • The synthetic test data for Hamburg and Bremen is in test-data/fdo-cca-demo; no data generation is needed.

Requirements

We found the following installation methods:

  • Python 3.10+
  • rdflib
  • nanopub (Python library for signing and publishing)
  • A nanopub profile (~/.nanopub/ or custom path)
mamba activate sciencelive  # or your env with rdflib + nanopub
source: README.md
×

Usage

Jupyter notebooks

Single record — notebooks/loom2nanopub.ipynb

Interactive workflow with preview before each publish step:

  1. Set LOOM_RESOURCE_ID in the Configuration cell
  2. Run all cells top to bottom
  3. Preview each TriG file before publishing
  4. Mark the record as DONE in loom_records.txt

Batch — notebooks/loom2nanopub_batch.ipynb

Process all non-DONE records:

  1. Run Setup cells (section 1)
  2. Run Generate — creates TriG files for all records into outputs/<ID>/
  3. Review the generated files
  4. Set PUBLISH_BATCH = True and run Publish

CLI script

# Single record
python loom2nanopub.py a03gjbxh5v

# All non-DONE records
python loom2nanopub.py --all

# Dry run (show what would be generated)
python loom2nanopub.py --all --dry-run

# Custom output directory
python loom2nanopub.py --all -o ./batch-output/

What gets extracted

The tools parse dtreg JSON-LD files from each record's GitLab repo and the Knowledge Loom API to produce nanopubs with:

Requirements

We found the following installation methods:

  • Python 3.10+
  • rdflib
  • nanopub (Python library for signing and publishing)
  • A nanopub profile (~/.nanopub/ or custom path)
mamba activate sciencelive  # or your env with rdflib + nanopub
source: README.md
×

Usage

Jupyter notebooks

Single record — notebooks/loom2nanopub.ipynb

Interactive workflow with preview before each publish step:

  1. Set LOOM_RESOURCE_ID in the Configuration cell
  2. Run all cells top to bottom
  3. Preview each TriG file before publishing
  4. Mark the record as DONE in loom_records.txt

Batch — notebooks/loom2nanopub_batch.ipynb

Process all non-DONE records:

  1. Run Setup cells (section 1)
  2. Run Generate — creates TriG files for all records into outputs/<ID>/
  3. Review the generated files
  4. Set PUBLISH_BATCH = True and run Publish

CLI script

# Single record
python loom2nanopub.py a03gjbxh5v

# All non-DONE records
python loom2nanopub.py --all

# Dry run (show what would be generated)
python loom2nanopub.py --all --dry-run

# Custom output directory
python loom2nanopub.py --all -o ./batch-output/

What gets extracted

The tools parse dtreg JSON-LD files from each record's GitLab repo and the Knowledge Loom API to produce nanopubs with:

Set up a Python environment

Requirements

We found the following installation methods:

  • Python 3.10 or later

source: README.md

Usage

RIOMAR ocean model (public, HEALPix DGGS)

python fdo2map.py https://w3id.org/ro-id/24600867-23ca-4b97-be14-3aa63883c056

Ocean temperature, salinity, and sea surface height from the GAMAR/GLORYS hindcast simulation, regridded to HEALPix level 13. Bay of Biscay, Oct–Dec 2023.

Sentinel-2 reflectance (public, HEALPix multiscale pyramid)

python fdo2map.py https://w3id.org/ro-id/fdc1c071-76d7-44df-a565-8217ebcc59fe

Sentinel-2 L1C Band 02 (Blue) reflectance on a HEALPix multiscale pyramid (levels 10–20, ~10km to ~10m resolution).

NorESM2 ARCTIC reanalysis (private, API key required)

python fdo2map.py https://w3id.org/ro-id/1f0b5044-ae4f-483d-b7a2-48a5a6ac3965

Monthly SST and 3D ocean temperature from NorESM2/BLOM (JRA-OC20 reanalysis), 2010–2018. Requires an API key — the script will prompt for it.

Usage

RIOMAR ocean model (public, HEALPix DGGS)

python fdo2map.py https://w3id.org/ro-id/24600867-23ca-4b97-be14-3aa63883c056

Ocean temperature, salinity, and sea surface height from the GAMAR/GLORYS hindcast simulation, regridded to HEALPix level 13. Bay of Biscay, Oct–Dec 2023.

Sentinel-2 reflectance (public, HEALPix multiscale pyramid)

python fdo2map.py https://w3id.org/ro-id/fdc1c071-76d7-44df-a565-8217ebcc59fe

Sentinel-2 L1C Band 02 (Blue) reflectance on a HEALPix multiscale pyramid (levels 10–20, ~10km to ~10m resolution).

NorESM2 ARCTIC reanalysis (private, API key required)

python fdo2map.py https://w3id.org/ro-id/1f0b5044-ae4f-483d-b7a2-48a5a6ac3965

Monthly SST and 3D ocean temperature from NorESM2/BLOM (JRA-OC20 reanalysis), 2010–2018. Requires an API key — the script will prompt for it.

Usage

Online demo

The Portugal Knowledge Dashboard is an initial prototype based on the CS4 design mockups. It presents metadata from three CS4 publication FDOs in ROHub, using recorded metadata snapshots, with configurable branding and styling for different case studies over a shared layout. Planned GitHub Pages address: https://fair2adapt.github.io/fdo-knowledge-dashboard/

Getting Started

Requirements: Python 3.12 and fdo-consume v1.1.0+.

git clone https://github.com/FAIR2Adapt/fdo-knowledge-dashboard.git
git clone https://github.com/FAIR2Adapt/fdo-consume.git
cd fdo-knowledge-dashboard

python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt ../fdo-consume

python server.py

Open http://localhost:8010.

Static Build

python scripts/build_site.py --config config/portugal-dashboard.yaml --out dist
python server.py --dist dist --port 8020

The generated site can be hosted on GitHub Pages or another static hosting service.

Usage

Online demo

The Portugal Knowledge Dashboard is an initial prototype based on the CS4 design mockups. It presents metadata from three CS4 publication FDOs in ROHub, using recorded metadata snapshots, with configurable branding and styling for different case studies over a shared layout. Planned GitHub Pages address: https://fair2adapt.github.io/fdo-knowledge-dashboard/

Getting Started

Requirements: Python 3.12 and fdo-consume v1.1.0+.

git clone https://github.com/FAIR2Adapt/fdo-knowledge-dashboard.git
git clone https://github.com/FAIR2Adapt/fdo-consume.git
cd fdo-knowledge-dashboard

python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt ../fdo-consume

python server.py

Open http://localhost:8010.

Static Build

python scripts/build_site.py --config config/portugal-dashboard.yaml --out dist
python server.py --dist dist --port 8020

The generated site can be hosted on GitHub Pages or another static hosting service.

DOI: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20448428
Version: 0.1.0
Released: 2026-05-29
License: Apache-2.0
Code: https://github.com/FAIR2Adapt/softwares_RIOMAR
Project: https://github.com/FAIR2Adapt/softwares_RIOMAR
Keywords: HEALPix, DGGS, regridding, ocean-model, xarray, kerchunk

Abstract:
Show abstract
End-to-end workflow to regrid ocean model data (RiOMar/GAMAR) from curvilinear grids to HEALPix (DGGS) format using xarray, Dask and Kerchunk, running both locally (HTTPS mode) and on HPC infrastructure. Part of the FAIR2Adapt initiative.
×

Installation

Installation

# 1. Create the conda environment  
conda env create -f notebook/environment.yml  
conda activate riomar  
  
# 2. Install the healpix_regrid package in editable mode  
pip install -e ".[test]"

B. Prepare a temporary Zarr (fast iteration dataset)

Notebook: Prep_regrid.ipynb

Purpose - Open RiOMar data via a Kerchunk catalog (HPC filesystem or
HTTPS export)\

  • Apply a spatial subset or mask using the ROI from step A\
  • Write a lightweight Zarr locally (or on HPC scratch) to speed up
    development

Output - A temporary Zarr dataset (e.g. small.zarr) used as input
for the regridding notebook

Tip - Set OUT_ZARR to an existing path on your machine or HPC
scratch.

End-to-end workflow to regrid ocean model data (RiOMar/GAMAR) from curvilinear grids to HEALPix (DGGS) format using xarray, Dask and Kerchunk, running both locally (HTTPS mode) and on HPC infrastructure. Part of the FAIR2Adapt initiative.
×

Installation

Installation

# 1. Create the conda environment  
conda env create -f notebook/environment.yml  
conda activate riomar  
  
# 2. Install the healpix_regrid package in editable mode  
pip install -e ".[test]"

B. Prepare a temporary Zarr (fast iteration dataset)

Notebook: Prep_regrid.ipynb

Purpose - Open RiOMar data via a Kerchunk catalog (HPC filesystem or
HTTPS export)\

  • Apply a spatial subset or mask using the ROI from step A\
  • Write a lightweight Zarr locally (or on HPC scratch) to speed up
    development

Output - A temporary Zarr dataset (e.g. small.zarr) used as input
for the regridding notebook

Tip - Set OUT_ZARR to an existing path on your machine or HPC
scratch.

Installation

Install

python3 -m venv .venv  
source .venv/bin/activate  
pip install .

Dependencies: PyYAML and PyLD (JSON-LD expansion; PyLD brings lxml, cachetools and frozendict). The RO-Crate contexts are bundled, so reading an object makes no network request unless source="live" is chosen.

source: README.md

Requirements

We found the following installation methods:

• pyproject.toml
×

Usage

from fdo_consume import consume

result = consume(
    "https://example.org/object/full",
    "map-panel-v1",
    recorded_dir="fixtures/example-profile",
    profile_maps="fixtures/example-profile/maps",      # external profile map; no code change required
    contracts="fixtures/example-profile/contracts",    # consumer-owned contracts
)

result.is_usable     # True if the contract is met and a binding is delivered
result.binding       # application-facing binding, or None
result.statuses      # resolution, validation, compatibility, and delivery
result.diagnostics   # diagnostics for FAIL, PARTIAL, or INDETERMINATE steps
result.record        # complete AccessRecord
result.summary()     # plain dict suitable for logging or UI presentation

Reading without a contract:

from fdo_consume import describe

record = describe("https://example.org/stand-in/hamburg-loom-record", recorded_dir="fixtures/cca-demo")
record.descriptor    # root fields, entities, resources, as the profile map reads them
record.validation    # profile conformance, judged apart from any consumer

A recorded folder holds pids.json ({"<pid>": {"fixture": "<name>"}}) and objects/<name>/ro-crate-metadata.json; payload files stay next to the crate. A resource inside the crate has the URL in-crate:<path>: the path is relative to that folder, and the library reads no payload bytes. An object that declares no profile IRI (the current Knowledge Loom export) is read with profile="knowledge-loom-0.1.0".

A contract names its consumer (service, capability), the needs (term, level must or should, an optional reason), the media types it accepts, and the overlay it needs (profile_additions); an optional source mapping may record where the needs come from. A term is a root field, an entity or a concept of a profile map (fdo_consume.profiles.known_terms); an overlay applies only to the map it extends, and the record's P2 step says when it was not applied.

    contracts="fixtures/example-profile/contracts",    # consumer-owned contracts
)

result.is_usable     # True if the contract is met and a binding is delivered
result.binding       # application-facing binding, or None
result.statuses      # resolution, validation, compatibility, and delivery
result.diagnostics   # diagnostics for FAIL, PARTIAL, or INDETERMINATE steps
result.record        # complete AccessRecord
result.summary()     # plain dict suitable for logging or UI presentation

Reading without a contract:

from fdo_consume import describe

record = describe("https://example.org/stand-in/hamburg-loom-record", recorded_dir="fixtures/cca-demo")
record.descriptor    # root fields, entities, resources, as the profile map reads them
record.validation    # profile conformance, judged apart from any consumer

A recorded folder holds pids.json ({"<pid>": {"fixture": "<name>"}}) and objects/<name>/ro-crate-metadata.json; payload files stay next to the crate. A resource inside the crate has the URL in-crate:<path>: the path is relative to that folder, and the library reads no payload bytes. An object that declares no profile IRI (the current Knowledge Loom export) is read with profile="knowledge-loom-0.1.0".

A contract names its consumer (service, capability), the needs (term, level must or should, an optional reason), the media types it accepts, and the overlay it needs (profile_additions); an optional source mapping may record where the needs come from. A term is a root field, an entity or a concept of a profile map (fdo_consume.profiles.known_terms); an overlay applies only to the map it extends, and the record's P2 step says when it was not applied.

Installation

Installation

# Clone the repo  
git clone https://github.com/FAIR2Adapt/climate-connectivity-taxonomy.git  
  
# Enter directory  
cd climate-connectivity-taxonomy  
  
# Install the Python dependencies  
pip install -r requirements.txt

Then choose how you want to look at the vocabulary.

Option A: build the public site locally (SkoHub Vocabs)

This builds exactly what is published on GitHub Pages, from the committed concepts.ttl and
methodology/. Nothing is fetched from the hub or Google.

# Normalise concepts.ttl, build the site with SkoHub and post-process it into public/  
bash scripts/build_site.sh  
  
# Serve it  
python3 -m http.server -d public 8000

Open http://localhost:8000/. The first build pulls the SkoHub image and takes a few minutes.

Option B: Skosmos preview locally

Skosmos is the internal tool for reviewing the vocabulary.

# Clone Skosmos into skosmos-src/, configure it, start Skosmos + Fuseki and load concepts.ttl  
bash .devcontainer/postCreate.sh

Open http://localhost:9090/ and click English. Stop it with
docker compose -f skosmos-src/docker-compose.yml down.

Option C: Skosmos preview in a GitHub Codespace

  1. In the GitHub repo, go to Code → Codespaces → Create codespace on main. This starts a VS
    Code environment and brings up Skosmos in Docker.

  2. Wait a few minutes for the containers to start. When they are ready, the terminal shows the
    Skosmos link.

  3. Open the link in a browser, then click English to view the taxonomy.

  4. If the container doesn't start, press F1 and run Codespaces: View creation log.

  5. When you're done, delete the Codespace (the free plan includes ~60 hours/month).

Requirements

We found the following installation methods:

• codemeta.json
• requirements.txt
You need nothing to browse or download the taxonomy. To build the site or run the preview yourself:
  • Linux, macOS or Windows with WSL2
  • Git
  • Docker with Docker Compose. The SkoHub image is linux/amd64-only; on Apple Silicon it runs under emulation (slower, but it works).
  • Python 3 (the CI uses 3.12) with rdflib 7.x, listed in requirements.txt
  • pandoc ≥ 3.1, for the methodology page of the site (option A only)
Alternatively, a GitHub account is enough to run the Skosmos preview in a GitHub Codespace, with nothing installed locally.
source: README.md
×

Usage

Reuse the vocabulary

concepts.ttl is plain SKOS in Turtle, so any RDF tool can read it:

from rdflib import Graph
g = Graph().parse("concepts.ttl")
print(len(g), "triples")

Each concept also has a human-readable page on the public site and a link back to the Connectivity Hub.

How the public site is kept up to date

Refreshing the data and deploying the site are separate steps, so a flaky hub (or Google) can never publish a truncated vocabulary or a broken page:

  1. refresh-vocab.yml runs every Monday, or by hand via Actions → Run workflow. Two independent jobs:

    • scripts/fetch_vocab.py crawls the hub through hasTopConcept/broader/narrower/related until it has every concept, retrying failures. The job commits concepts.ttl only if the fetch is complete.
    • scripts/fetch_methodology.sh takes a copy of the methodology Google Doc (which the hub team keeps editing) into methodology/, and commits it only if the content changed.

    If either job committed, the workflow then starts the deploy.

  2. pages.yml runs scripts/build_site.sh on the committed files and deploys the result to GitHub Pages. It never contacts the hub or Google. Run it by hand to rebuild the site without new data. Pull requests run the build without deploying and attach the built site as a site-preview artifact.

build_site.sh normalises the vocabulary for SkoHub (prepare_vocab.py: licence, symmetric broader/narrower, same-language de-duplication), builds the site with the skohub/skohub-vocabs-docker image plus small patches (scripts/patch_*.sh), then sorts and re-indents the navigation tree (sort_tree.py, fix_tree_indent.py), and renders the methodology page from methodology/ with pandoc (render_methodology.sh).

So concepts.ttl is always the last complete published vocabulary, and git log -- concepts.ttl and git log -- methodology/ show how the taxonomy and its methodology changed over time. Don't edit methodology/ by hand: edit the Google Doc.

To fetch the current vocabulary from the hub yourself:

python3 scripts/fetch_vocab.py concepts.ttl

Installation

Installation

# Clone the repo  
git clone https://github.com/FAIR2Adapt/climate-connectivity-taxonomy.git  
  
# Enter directory  
cd climate-connectivity-taxonomy  
  
# Install the Python dependencies  
pip install -r requirements.txt

Then choose how you want to look at the vocabulary.

Option A: build the public site locally (SkoHub Vocabs)

This builds exactly what is published on GitHub Pages, from the committed concepts.ttl and
methodology/. Nothing is fetched from the hub or Google.

# Normalise concepts.ttl, build the site with SkoHub and post-process it into public/  
bash scripts/build_site.sh  
  
# Serve it  
python3 -m http.server -d public 8000

Open http://localhost:8000/. The first build pulls the SkoHub image and takes a few minutes.

Option B: Skosmos preview locally

Skosmos is the internal tool for reviewing the vocabulary.

# Clone Skosmos into skosmos-src/, configure it, start Skosmos + Fuseki and load concepts.ttl  
bash .devcontainer/postCreate.sh

Open http://localhost:9090/ and click English. Stop it with
docker compose -f skosmos-src/docker-compose.yml down.

Option C: Skosmos preview in a GitHub Codespace

  1. In the GitHub repo, go to Code → Codespaces → Create codespace on main. This starts a VS
    Code environment and brings up Skosmos in Docker.

  2. Wait a few minutes for the containers to start. When they are ready, the terminal shows the
    Skosmos link.

  3. Open the link in a browser, then click English to view the taxonomy.

  4. If the container doesn't start, press F1 and run Codespaces: View creation log.

  5. When you're done, delete the Codespace (the free plan includes ~60 hours/month).

source: README.md

Requirements

We found the following installation methods:

• codemeta.json
• requirements.txt
You need nothing to browse or download the taxonomy. To build the site or run the preview yourself:
  • Linux, macOS or Windows with WSL2
  • Git
  • Docker with Docker Compose. The SkoHub image is linux/amd64-only; on Apple Silicon it runs under emulation (slower, but it works).
  • Python 3 (the CI uses 3.12) with rdflib 7.x, listed in requirements.txt
  • pandoc ≥ 3.1, for the methodology page of the site (option A only)
Alternatively, a GitHub account is enough to run the Skosmos preview in a GitHub Codespace, with nothing installed locally.
source: README.md
×

Usage

Reuse the vocabulary

concepts.ttl is plain SKOS in Turtle, so any RDF tool can read it:

from rdflib import Graph
g = Graph().parse("concepts.ttl")
print(len(g), "triples")

Each concept also has a human-readable page on the public site and a link back to the Connectivity Hub.

How the public site is kept up to date

Refreshing the data and deploying the site are separate steps, so a flaky hub (or Google) can never publish a truncated vocabulary or a broken page:

  1. refresh-vocab.yml runs every Monday, or by hand via Actions → Run workflow. Two independent jobs:

    • scripts/fetch_vocab.py crawls the hub through hasTopConcept/broader/narrower/related until it has every concept, retrying failures. The job commits concepts.ttl only if the fetch is complete.
    • scripts/fetch_methodology.sh takes a copy of the methodology Google Doc (which the hub team keeps editing) into methodology/, and commits it only if the content changed.

    If either job committed, the workflow then starts the deploy.

  2. pages.yml runs scripts/build_site.sh on the committed files and deploys the result to GitHub Pages. It never contacts the hub or Google. Run it by hand to rebuild the site without new data. Pull requests run the build without deploying and attach the built site as a site-preview artifact.

build_site.sh normalises the vocabulary for SkoHub (prepare_vocab.py: licence, symmetric broader/narrower, same-language de-duplication), builds the site with the skohub/skohub-vocabs-docker image plus small patches (scripts/patch_*.sh), then sorts and re-indents the navigation tree (sort_tree.py, fix_tree_indent.py), and renders the methodology page from methodology/ with pandoc (render_methodology.sh).

So concepts.ttl is always the last complete published vocabulary, and git log -- concepts.ttl and git log -- methodology/ show how the taxonomy and its methodology changed over time. Don't edit methodology/ by hand: edit the Google Doc.

To fetch the current vocabulary from the hub yourself:

python3 scripts/fetch_vocab.py concepts.ttl

Abstract:
Show abstract
A method and open-source implementation for expressing and enforcing access to sensitive FAIR Digital Objects, combining ODRL policies, nanopublication-based access grants, Decentralized Identifiers (DIDs) and authenticated encryption (AES-256-GCM with ECDH/HKDF key wrapping). Developed in the FAIR2Adapt project for controlled-access climate change adaptation data.

Usage

Data provider workflow

# 1. Generate a keypair for your DID
fair-data-access keygen -d ~/.fair-data-access/

# 2. Create a DID document (served via GitHub Pages)
fair-data-access did-doc did:web:fair2adapt.github.io:fair-data-access public_key.pem

# 3. Create an ODRL policy
fair-data-access policy \
  --uid "https://fair2adapt.eu/policy/hamburg-buildings" \
  --target "https://fair2adapt.eu/data/hamburg-buildings" \
  --permit-actions use reproduce \
  --prohibit-actions distribute commercialize \
  --purpose https://w3id.org/dpv#AcademicResearch \
  --require-attribution \
  -o policies/hamburg-buildings.jsonld

# 4. Encrypt your data
fair-data-access encrypt buildings.gpkg --save-key dataset_key.txt

# 5. Upload encrypted data to Zenodo/S3
# 6. Store dataset_key.txt content as a GitHub Secret (KEY_HAMBURG_BUILDINGS)
# 7. Publish ODRL policy as nanopub via Nanodash template (see below)
# 8. Update policies/registry.json with the nanopub URI

Publishing ODRL policies via Nanodash

Policies should be created via the Nanodash template forms to ensure compatibility:

  • Policy template: Create ODRL Access Policy
  • Grant template: Create ODRL Access Grant

The nanopubs/ directory also contains notebooks for programmatic template creation and retraction.

Data consumer workflow

# 1. Generate your DID keypair
fair-data-access keygen -d ~/.fair-data-access/

# 2. Set up did:web (serve did.json at your domain)
fair-data-access did-doc did:web:myuni.edu:me public_key.pem

# 3. Open an access request issue on GitHub
#    (use the issue template at the data-access repo)

# 4. After approval, download and decrypt
curl -o wrapped_key.json https://fair2adapt.github.io/fair-data-access/keys/<did-hash>/hamburg-buildings.key
fair-data-access decrypt buildings.gpkg.enc -k <unwrapped-key>

Integration with urban_pfr pipeline

In FDO mode, the pipeline can automatically handle encrypted inputs:

from fair_data_access import decrypt_file, evaluate_policy, fetch_policy
from fair_data_access.keys import unwrap_key
from fair_data_access.rocrate import load_encrypted_input

# crate_entry: the encrypted file's entry in ro-crate-metadata.json
data = load_encrypted_input(
    crate_entry,
    private_key_pem=open("my_private_key.pem", "rb").read(),
    requester_did="did:web:example.org:me",
    dataset="hamburg-buildings",  # fetches {keyServer}/keys/{sha256(DID)}/hamburg-buildings.key
)

Crates built with add_encrypted_file_to_crate() declare their access terms in @context (hasPolicy = odrl:hasPolicy, also used for grants, which are odrl:Agreement policies; accessRights = dct:accessRights with the EU value RESTRICTED; and contentEncryption, encryptionAlgorithm, keyServer under https://w3id.org/sciencelive/o/terms/, each defined by a nanopublication), so the policy link survives JSON-LD processing.

Abstract:
Show abstract
A method and open-source implementation for expressing and enforcing access to sensitive FAIR Digital Objects, combining ODRL policies, nanopublication-based access grants, Decentralized Identifiers (DIDs) and authenticated encryption (AES-256-GCM with ECDH/HKDF key wrapping). Developed in the FAIR2Adapt project for controlled-access climate change adaptation data.

Usage

Data provider workflow

# 1. Generate a keypair for your DID
fair-data-access keygen -d ~/.fair-data-access/

# 2. Create a DID document (served via GitHub Pages)
fair-data-access did-doc did:web:fair2adapt.github.io:fair-data-access public_key.pem

# 3. Create an ODRL policy
fair-data-access policy \
  --uid "https://fair2adapt.eu/policy/hamburg-buildings" \
  --target "https://fair2adapt.eu/data/hamburg-buildings" \
  --permit-actions use reproduce \
  --prohibit-actions distribute commercialize \
  --purpose https://w3id.org/dpv#AcademicResearch \
  --require-attribution \
  -o policies/hamburg-buildings.jsonld

# 4. Encrypt your data
fair-data-access encrypt buildings.gpkg --save-key dataset_key.txt

# 5. Upload encrypted data to Zenodo/S3
# 6. Store dataset_key.txt content as a GitHub Secret (KEY_HAMBURG_BUILDINGS)
# 7. Publish ODRL policy as nanopub via Nanodash template (see below)
# 8. Update policies/registry.json with the nanopub URI

Publishing ODRL policies via Nanodash

Policies should be created via the Nanodash template forms to ensure compatibility:

  • Policy template: Create ODRL Access Policy
  • Grant template: Create ODRL Access Grant

The nanopubs/ directory also contains notebooks for programmatic template creation and retraction.

Data consumer workflow

# 1. Generate your DID keypair
fair-data-access keygen -d ~/.fair-data-access/

# 2. Set up did:web (serve did.json at your domain)
fair-data-access did-doc did:web:myuni.edu:me public_key.pem

# 3. Open an access request issue on GitHub
#    (use the issue template at the data-access repo)

# 4. After approval, download and decrypt
curl -o wrapped_key.json https://fair2adapt.github.io/fair-data-access/keys/<did-hash>/hamburg-buildings.key
fair-data-access decrypt buildings.gpkg.enc -k <unwrapped-key>

Integration with urban_pfr pipeline

In FDO mode, the pipeline can automatically handle encrypted inputs:

from fair_data_access import decrypt_file, evaluate_policy, fetch_policy
from fair_data_access.keys import unwrap_key
from fair_data_access.rocrate import load_encrypted_input

# crate_entry: the encrypted file's entry in ro-crate-metadata.json
data = load_encrypted_input(
    crate_entry,
    private_key_pem=open("my_private_key.pem", "rb").read(),
    requester_did="did:web:example.org:me",
    dataset="hamburg-buildings",  # fetches {keyServer}/keys/{sha256(DID)}/hamburg-buildings.key
)

Crates built with add_encrypted_file_to_crate() declare their access terms in @context (hasPolicy = odrl:hasPolicy, also used for grants, which are odrl:Agreement policies; accessRights = dct:accessRights with the EU value RESTRICTED; and contentEncryption, encryptionAlgorithm, keyServer under https://w3id.org/sciencelive/o/terms/, each defined by a nanopublication), so the policy link survives JSON-LD processing.

Usage

Basic: resolve data crates to workflow inputs

from fdo_resolver import FDOResolver

# Load input slots from a Workflow RO-Crate
resolver = FDOResolver.from_workflow_crate("path/to/workflow-rocrate/")

# Resolve data crates against the workflow profile
result = resolver.resolve("path/to/input-data/")

print(result.is_complete)  # True if all required inputs matched
print(result.paths)        # {param_name: Path(...), ...}
print(result.summary())    # Human-readable summary

Variable-level matching with I-ADOPT

When input datasets describe their columns via variableMeasured (using schema.org PropertyValue with propertyID pointing to semantic identifiers like I-ADOPT nanopublications), the resolver can match columns between workflow expectations and data offerings.

Workflow RO-Crate declares expected variables:

{
  "@id": "#param-buildings",
  "@type": "FormalParameter",
  "name": "buildings",
  "encodingFormat": "application/flatgeobuf",
  "variableMeasured": [
    {"@id": "#expected-elderly-singles"}
  ]
}

{
  "@id": "#expected-elderly-singles",
  "@type": "PropertyValue",
  "name": "elderly_singles",
  "propertyID": "https://w3id.org/np/RA...",
  "additionalType": "sensitivity_indicator"
}

Data RO-Crate describes its columns:

{
  "@id": "buildings.fgb",
  "@type": "File",
  "encodingFormat": "application/flatgeobuf",
  "variableMeasured": [
    {"@id": "#var-es"}
  ]
}

{
  "@id": "#var-es",
  "@type": "PropertyValue",
  "name": "ES",
  "propertyID": "https://w3id.org/np/RA..."
}

Resolve and get column mappings:

result = resolver.resolve("path/to/input-data/")

# Get the column mapping for the buildings input
binding = result.bindings["buildings"]
print(binding.column_mapping)
# {"elderly_singles": "ES"}
# workflow expects "elderly_singles" → data has it as column "ES"

The propertyID (e.g. an I-ADOPT nanopublication URI) is the semantic key that connects the workflow's expected variable to the data's actual column name. This allows different cities to use different column names while the workflow remains generic.

Programmatic parameter definitions

resolver = FDOResolver.from_parameters([
    {
        "name": "buildings",
        "encoding_format": "application/flatgeobuf",
        "variables_measured": [
            {
                "name": "elderly_singles",
                "property_id": "https://w3id.org/np/RA...",
                "role": "sensitivity_indicator",
            },
        ],
    },
    {
        "name": "flood_levels",
        "encoding_format": "application/geo+json",
        "additional_type": "https://example.org/FloodLevelCollection",
    },
])

result = resolver.resolve("path/to/input-data/")

Usage

Basic: resolve data crates to workflow inputs

from fdo_resolver import FDOResolver

# Load input slots from a Workflow RO-Crate
resolver = FDOResolver.from_workflow_crate("path/to/workflow-rocrate/")

# Resolve data crates against the workflow profile
result = resolver.resolve("path/to/input-data/")

print(result.is_complete)  # True if all required inputs matched
print(result.paths)        # {param_name: Path(...), ...}
print(result.summary())    # Human-readable summary

Variable-level matching with I-ADOPT

When input datasets describe their columns via variableMeasured (using schema.org PropertyValue with propertyID pointing to semantic identifiers like I-ADOPT nanopublications), the resolver can match columns between workflow expectations and data offerings.

Workflow RO-Crate declares expected variables:

{
  "@id": "#param-buildings",
  "@type": "FormalParameter",
  "name": "buildings",
  "encodingFormat": "application/flatgeobuf",
  "variableMeasured": [
    {"@id": "#expected-elderly-singles"}
  ]
}

{
  "@id": "#expected-elderly-singles",
  "@type": "PropertyValue",
  "name": "elderly_singles",
  "propertyID": "https://w3id.org/np/RA...",
  "additionalType": "sensitivity_indicator"
}

Data RO-Crate describes its columns:

{
  "@id": "buildings.fgb",
  "@type": "File",
  "encodingFormat": "application/flatgeobuf",
  "variableMeasured": [
    {"@id": "#var-es"}
  ]
}

{
  "@id": "#var-es",
  "@type": "PropertyValue",
  "name": "ES",
  "propertyID": "https://w3id.org/np/RA..."
}

Resolve and get column mappings:

result = resolver.resolve("path/to/input-data/")

# Get the column mapping for the buildings input
binding = result.bindings["buildings"]
print(binding.column_mapping)
# {"elderly_singles": "ES"}
# workflow expects "elderly_singles" → data has it as column "ES"

The propertyID (e.g. an I-ADOPT nanopublication URI) is the semantic key that connects the workflow's expected variable to the data's actual column name. This allows different cities to use different column names while the workflow remains generic.

Programmatic parameter definitions

resolver = FDOResolver.from_parameters([
    {
        "name": "buildings",
        "encoding_format": "application/flatgeobuf",
        "variables_measured": [
            {
                "name": "elderly_singles",
                "property_id": "https://w3id.org/np/RA...",
                "role": "sensitivity_indicator",
            },
        ],
    },
    {
        "name": "flood_levels",
        "encoding_format": "application/geo+json",
        "additional_type": "https://example.org/FloodLevelCollection",
    },
])

result = resolver.resolve("path/to/input-data/")
